name: Junction control and conflict models (fixed-time, actuated and adaptive signals incl. CoSiCoSt; gap acceptance at unsignalised junctions; roundabouts; conflict points)
type: model (junction right-of-way, conflict resolution and signal control models, with Indian parameter values)
maintainer: Reference implementations: Eclipse SUMO (DLR / Eclipse Foundation) and traffic-simulation.de / MovSim (Martin Treiber, Arne Kesting). Indian parameters: CSIR-CRRI Indo-HCM 2017 and academic groups (e.g. Kota, Pallela and Lalam, NIT Warangal 2025; Ashalatha and Chandra 2011). Signal guidance: Indian Roads Congress (IRC:93-1985). Indian adaptive control: CoSiCoSt by C-DAC Thiruvananthapuram with KELTRON
first_release: IRC:93 signal guidelines 1985; Ashalatha and Chandra clearing-behaviour critical gap 2011; Indo-HCM 2017; SUMO junction model with internal lanes long-standing (internal junctions customisable since SUMO 0.25.0); CoSiCoSt deployed in Pune by about 2012 [uncertain]
last_activity: Checked 2026-11-11: SUMO docs current (Intersections, Traffic Lights, vType junction-model parameters); traffic-simulation.de repo active (550 commits, no dated release); Kota et al. Warangal gap study published 2025; Bengaluru B-ATCS (adaptive signals) reported in an April 2026 case study
licence: SUMO EPL-2.0; traffic-simulation.de GPL-3.0; Indo-HCM and IRC codes are copyrighted publications (numbers are facts and may be used); CoSiCoSt is proprietary (C-DAC, licensed to integrators such as DIMTS)
language: SUMO C++; traffic-simulation.de JavaScript; CoSiCoSt runs on C-DAC CUTE controllers (implementation language not published) [uncertain]
code_availability: SUMO source: github.com/eclipse-sumo/sumo (junction logic in src/microsim/MSLink.cpp). traffic-simulation.de source: github.com/movsim/traffic-simulation-de (road.connect / determineConflicts in js/road.js, README_intersections). Indian gap and saturation-flow values: papers and Indo-HCM manual only. CoSiCoSt: no public code or specification, only presentations and trade-press descriptions
maintenance_health: SUMO junction model is actively maintained and heavily parameterised. traffic-simulation.de intersection logic is maintained by one author and its README says turns are 'not yet perfect'. Indian critical gap literature is fragmented across many small single-city studies with differing methods (Raff, occupation time, clearing behaviour, MLE). CoSiCoSt is maintained commercially by C-DAC; algorithm internals are not published
scale: Microscopic (vehicle-level conflict resolution); signal-timing formulas (Webster, Indo-HCM saturation flow) are macroscopic inputs
car_following: Junction logic sits on top of car-following: in SUMO a closed link is a standing obstacle at the stop line (vehicles at traffic lights wait 1 m before lane end, jmStoplineGap = 1 m; minor-road vehicles wait exactly at lane end, jmStoplineGapMinor = 0 m). In traffic-simulation.de a red light or a stop sign is a virtual zero-length standing vehicle per lane, so IDM produces the braking; a crossing vehicle is assumed to accelerate freely with the IDM acceleration a when computing its crossing time
lane_model: SUMO: each connection (link) from an incoming lane to an outgoing lane has its own internal lane(s) through the junction; left turners from the major road can be split by an internal junction so they wait inside the box (cont=1). traffic-simulation.de: connections are road.connect(target, uSource, uTarget, offsetLane, conflicts, options) between directed road objects; turns without conflicts behave like single-point merges/diverges
lateral_model_type: None inside the junction in both reference implementations (vehicles follow the connector centreline). Indian practice of fanning out across the junction box is not modelled by either
junction_model: SUMO (implementable rules): (1) netconvert builds a right-of-way matrix per junction: each connection has request index, a 'response' bitstring (higher-priority connections it must yield to), a 'foes' bitstring (all conflicting connections, superset of response) and 'cont' (may enter and wait at an internal junction). Bitstrings are read right to left. (2) Connection states: M major, m minor, = equal, G/g green major/minor, r red, y/Y yellow, o flashing, O off, plus zipper (Z) at merge junctions and stop/all-way-stop types. (3) Each approaching vehicle registers its expected arrival and leave times on the link it will use; a minor vehicle may enter only if no foe in 'response' would arrive within its occupation window, keeping at least jmTimegapMinor = 1 s before/after a prioritised vehicle that has not yet entered; jmAdvance = 1 lets it creep to the conflict point when a foe is already inside. (4) Keep-clear: vehicles do not enter if they would be stuck inside (default.junctions.keep-clear = true); jmIgnoreKeepClearTime = -1 (never ignore) by default. (5) Driver imperfection: impatience (0 default) grows willingness to force priority; jmIgnoreFoeProb / jmIgnoreFoeSpeed allow ignoring slow priority foes; jmDriveAfterRedTime / jmDriveAfterYellowTime allow red/yellow running; jmExtraGap adds distance a foe must clear. (6) Turn speed limited by sqrt(radius * 5.5). (7) Minor vehicles decide brake-or-go at the connection's visibilityDistance. traffic-simulation.de (simpler, implementable in a day): connections carry explicit conflict lists derived from rule sets (priority road, right-before-left, signals). A secondary vehicle may go only if C1: the crossing area is not occupied by a main-road vehicle, AND C2: the lowest anticipated time-to-collision exceeds TTC_crit of about 3 s, with t_cross = sqrt(2 s_cross / a_IDM), s_min = s_main - v_main * t_cross, TTC = s_min / v_main. Without stop signs the test is applied at a decision point 20-50 m upstream; if it fails the vehicle stops at a virtual obstacle at the stop line. Right turns (for right-hand traffic) have no conflicts; straight across a main road conflicts with both main directions; left turn from priority road conflicts with opposite straight traffic. Roundabouts are modelled as a ring road with on-ramps (yield at entry) and off-ramps per arm. Recommended rule set for our engine: precompute conflict points as intersections of connector centrelines (widened by vehicle half-widths) at each node; each vehicle approaching reserves a time window [t_in, t_out] at each conflict point on its connector; a lower-priority vehicle enters only if no higher-priority reservation overlaps its window extended by the class-specific critical gap; apply keep-clear (exit link has room for the vehicle length) and an impatience term so long-waiting vehicles accept smaller gaps (forced entry, as observed in India)
signal_control_modes: Fixed-time: SUMO netconvert default program is a 90 s cycle with green split equally between main phases (about 31 s each at a 4-arm junction), yellow from approach speed, protected left phase 6 s if needed. Webster optimum cycle C0 = (1.5L + 5)/(1 - Y) is the classic design formula used in Indian practice; IRC:93-1985 is reported to bound cycles at 40-120 s with 60-90 s optimum [uncertain: secondary summary], but observed Indian cycles are often longer: 4-phase pre-timed signals of 125 s, 142 s (morning) and 167 s (evening) in Ahmedabad/Surat, 120 s fixed-time junctions in Kerala, and a 180 s cycle at Hoodi/KR Puram in Bengaluru [uncertain: student poster]. Common Indian phase plan is split phasing (one approach at a time, all movements), which the Ahmedabad/Surat 4-phase sites illustrate [uncertain as a general rule]. Actuated: SUMO gap-based actuated control with max-gap 3.0 s, detector-gap 2.0 s, passing-time 2.0 s, generated minDur 5 s / maxDur 50 s; delay_based (minTimeLoss 1 s); NEMA. Adaptive: CoSiCoSt (C-DAC Thiruvananthapuram + KELTRON) is the indigenous Indian ATCS, designed for heterogeneous traffic with poor lane discipline; publicly described as optimising signal timings in real time through a weighted combination of delay and stops, using second-by-second detector data and time-stamped phase terminations, coordinating by comparing phase-termination timestamps to correct offset deviations, and selecting routes dynamically instead of time-of-day plans; vendor material claims no separate advance detectors are needed. Runs on C-DAC CUTE / Wi-TraC controllers with modes fixed-time, semi-actuated, vehicle-actuated and ATCS. Deployments reported in Pune (38, later 67 junctions), Jaipur, Kolkata, Ahmedabad, Bhubaneswar, Hyderabad; algorithm internals are not published [uncertain]. Learned control: SUMO TraCI hooks; no Indian standard exists
flyover_support: N/A for this item (see B07). Relevant link: the at-grade junction under a flyover is a normal signalised junction with reduced approach width
vehicle_types: SUMO lets every junction-model parameter (jm*, impatience) be set per vType, so 2W/3W/car/bus can have different gap acceptance and red-running behaviour. Indian studies consistently find two- and three-wheelers accept the smallest gaps and heavy vehicles the largest, and that the share of large vehicles in the conflicting stream raises the critical gap
gridlock_policy: SUMO: keep-clear heuristic (on by default) to avoid blocking the box; --ignore-junction-blocker TIME to ignore blockers after TIME; jmIgnoreKeepClearTime per vType; teleporting of vehicles stuck longer than time-to-teleport (default 300 s) is reported in the summary output [uncertain: default value from memory, see SUMO docs]. traffic-simulation.de has a separate gridlock note (README_Gridlock). A/B Street prevents blocked boxes and documents gridlock handling separately. Our build: implement keep-clear plus an impatience-based forced entry, and report any deadlock-breaking action as a metric (see the Gridlock item)
mixed_traffic_support: Partial in references: SUMO supports per-class parameters but its foe logic assumes vehicles follow connector centrelines. Indian evidence shows small vehicles fill gaps laterally inside the junction and force entry (Ashalatha and Chandra found forced entry has a substantial effect on minor-approach capacity), so a pure gap-acceptance model underestimates minor-street capacity in India
non_lane_behaviour: Inside Indian junctions, vehicles do not follow lane-to-lane connectors; they spread across the box, creep into conflict areas and negotiate priority by forcing (priority reversal). Indian methodology responded with occupation-time and clearing-behaviour methods instead of classical lag/gap methods: Kota et al. (2025) measured conflict-area occupation times (2W shortest, heavy vehicles longest, e.g. minimum occupation 2.0-3.4 s for 2W and 6.6-12.6 s for HV across five Warangal intersections). Practical model: let a vehicle enter if its class-specific critical gap is met OR its waiting time exceeds a threshold and the foe is slow (SUMO-style impatience / jmIgnoreFoeProb), and give conflict points a lateral extent so 2W can pass beside a waiting car
seepage_filtering_support: Junction models in SUMO and traffic-simulation.de have no seepage. SUMO offers stopOffset per vehicle class (e.g. bike boxes) which can emulate 2W stopping ahead of cars at the stop line. Seepage itself is covered by the strip-based seepage item; at the junction the effect is a larger first-discharge platoon of 2W and a higher saturation flow per metre
per_class_parameters: Critical gap tc and follow-up time tf (s) at five urban uncontrolled intersections, Warangal (Kota, Pallela, Lalam 2025, Raff's method; tf assumed 0.6 tc, not measured): 2W tc 3.1/3.4/4.1/3.4/3.3, tf 1.86/2.04/2.46/2.04/1.98; 3W tc 3.2/4.0/4.3/3.4/3.8, tf 1.92/2.40/2.58/2.04/2.28; car tc 3.9/5.3/5.0/5.0/3.9, tf 2.34/3.18/3.00/3.00/2.34; LCV tc 3.6/4.0/4.8/4.8/4.3; overall tc 3.3-4.3. At intersection III the paper reports heavy vehicles 4.4 s and rejecting gaps up to 9 s. Other Indian reports: right-turning 2W temporal critical gap 2.8-3.9 s depending on method [uncertain: secondary snippet]; Indian four-legged uncontrolled intersections with critical gaps below 4 s (Maurya et al. 2016, cited by Kota). Roundabouts per Indo-HCM 2017 as cited by a calibration study: tc 2.00 s / tf 1.50 s for 20-30 m diameter and 1.90 s / 1.40 s for 30-40 m [uncertain: secondary]. For comparison, US HCM 2000 base values for a passenger car are about 4.1 s (major left) to 7.1 s (minor left across two-lane major) critical headway with 2.2-3.5 s follow-up [uncertain: from memory of HCM 2000 Exhibit 17-5; source linked]. Saturation flow per metre of approach width (Indo-HCM 2017 as quoted in a WCTR 2019 paper): 630 PCU/h/m for w < 7.0 m; (1140 - 60w) PCU/h/m for 7.0-10.5 m; 500 PCU/h/m for w > 10.5 m. Example: a 7.0 m approach gives 7 x 720 = 5040 PCU/h of green; 10.5 m gives 10.5 x 510 = 5355 PCU/h; note the step at 7.0 m (6.99 m gives about 4400) which suggests either a transcription issue or a deliberate regime change [uncertain]. Classic Webster/Road Note 34 width formula s = 525w PCU/h used in older Indian practice [uncertain]
indian_calibration_evidence: Kota, Pallela and Lalam (2025): five uncontrolled intersections in Warangal, video data, critical gaps by Raff's method per class, occupation time per class, capacity by Indo-HCM; found occupation time of minor approach increases 0.2 s per 5% increase in conflicting-flow occupation and 0.13 s per 5% pedestrian volume increase. Ashalatha and Chandra (2011, KSCE J. Civil Eng. 15:1427-1434): clearing-behaviour approach for critical gap, forced entry substantial. Saturation-flow calibrations at Indian signals show high errors when US HCM equations are applied to heterogeneous traffic and propose modified base saturation flow including 2W effect (WCTR 2019). Maji, Maurya, Nama and Sahu (Journal of Modern Transportation, 2015): microsimulation of intersection layouts under a flyover for heterogeneous traffic
calibration_dataset_used: Video recordings at five intersections in Warangal (Kota et al. 2025, not open); field discharge counts at Indian signalised intersections (WCTR 2019 paper, not open); Ahmedabad and Surat 4-phase pre-timed signals (Springer chapter, not open). No open Indian junction trajectory dataset was found for this item [uncertain]
calibration_method: Critical gap: Raff's method (cumulative accepted vs rejected gap curves), clearing-behaviour approach, occupation-time method, maximum likelihood and probability equilibrium methods; deterministic methods give lower values than probabilistic ones in a high-speed T-intersection study. Follow-up often assumed as 0.6 x critical gap instead of measured. Saturation flow: headway/discharge analysis per cycle with ANOVA to identify the saturated part of green, then multiple linear regression for base saturation flow and adjustment factors; error metric percent difference between observed and estimated saturation flow
max_density_tested: Not reported for junction models; studies report flows and capacities, not densities
validation_against_field_case: Warangal five uncontrolled intersections (capacity by Indo-HCM using measured critical gaps); Ahmedabad/Surat 4-phase pre-timed signals (cycles 125-167 s); Hoodi/KR Puram Bengaluru 180 s cycle re-timed to 150 s by Webster [uncertain: student poster]; CoSiCoSt Pune deployment with a reported about 50% congestion reduction at major junctions, measurement method not stated [uncertain]
reuse_mode: Port the model, not the code: adopt SUMO's foe/response matrix plus time-window reservation and keep-clear concepts, traffic-simulation.de's TTC-based gap rule and virtual-obstacle stop lines, Indian per-class critical gaps from Kota et al. as defaults, and Indo-HCM saturation flow per metre as a calibration target for signalised approaches. CoSiCoSt cannot be reused (proprietary, undocumented); offer an 'adaptive (CoSiCoSt-like)' mode that re-splits green each cycle by measured degree of saturation and clearly label it as an approximation
effort_within_72_hours: About 10-14 hours total. 3-4 h: connector geometry and precomputed conflict points per node with priority (major/minor/equal, signal group). 3-4 h: reservation-window gap acceptance with per-class tc/tf, keep-clear check, impatience-based forced entry. 2-3 h: fixed-time signal programs (cycle, phases, amber 3 s, all-red) with split phasing presets and Webster auto-timing from demand using Indo-HCM saturation flow. 1-2 h: simple actuated mode (max-gap 3 s, minDur/maxDur). 1 h: roundabout as a ring of links with yield-at-entry using the same gap logic. Cut: NEMA, coordinated offsets, real CoSiCoSt logic, pedestrian crossings, internal waiting positions beyond one per left/right turn
licence_constraint: Reading SUMO (EPL-2.0) and traffic-simulation.de (GPL-3.0) to re-implement algorithms is fine; copying traffic-simulation.de code would force our engine to GPL-3.0 if distributed; copying SUMO code requires EPL-2.0 file-level terms. Published numeric parameters (Indo-HCM, papers) are facts and can be used with citation. CoSiCoSt branding should not be used to describe our approximation
known_limitations: SUMO junction logic assumes lane-following vehicles on connectors; with the sublane model foes are still link-based, so Indian box-filling and creeping are not captured. traffic-simulation.de's TTC rule is acknowledged as defensive (sometimes blocks a start even after the threat passed) and its left-turn handling is 'not yet perfect'; its intersection README covers straight-only X intersections and excludes signals. Indian critical gaps vary widely by site (car 3.9-5.3 s across five intersections in one city), follow-up is often assumed rather than measured, and methods disagree. Indo-HCM saturation flow uses width only and has limited ability to address heterogeneity; the per-metre formula appears discontinuous at 7.0 m. CoSiCoSt internals, parameters and evaluation methodology are not public; reported benefits are vendor or trade-press claims
documented_failures: SUMO networks imported from OSM commonly produce junction deadlocks and teleports when many minor links conflict and keep-clear or join settings are wrong (see the Gridlock item and SUMO Intersections docs on ignore-junction-blocker). Applying US HCM saturation flow or gap values in India gives large errors due to heterogeneous traffic (WCTR 2019). Most Indian fixed-time signals keep the same timings for years without revision, so static plans mismatch demand (arXiv 2205.01640). Traffic under flyovers is often left unmanaged, which erodes the flyover's benefit (Maji et al. 2015)
validation_approach: SUMO: extensive regression test suite and documented parameter semantics. traffic-simulation.de: visual plausibility in interactive scenarios. Indian studies: compare estimated capacity or saturation flow against field counts (percent error), cumulative accepted/rejected gap curves. For our build: unit tests per junction type (two-car T-junction, crossing, opposite left turn), check discharge rate of a saturated signal approach against Indo-HCM PCU/h/m for the drawn width, and check that minor-approach capacity falls with conflicting flow in the shape predicted by gap-acceptance theory
takeaway_for_our_build: 1) Model each node as a set of connectors with precomputed conflict points and a priority relation (SUMO-style response/foes), and resolve conflicts by time-window reservation, not by geometry checks every step. 2) Use per-class critical gaps as defaults: 2W 3.5 s, 3W 3.7 s, car 4.6 s, LCV 4.3 s (five-site means from Kota et al. 2025), bus/truck about 5.0 s (extrapolated from the 4.4 s single-site value and the larger-vehicle trend [uncertain]), follow-up = 0.6 x critical gap, plus an impatience rule that shrinks the gap after about 10-20 s waiting [uncertain value] to reproduce Indian forced entry. 3) Always enforce keep-clear (do not enter unless the exit link has space) and report every forced resolution. 4) Signals: default to split phasing (one approach per phase) with amber 3 s and all-red 2 s [uncertain values], cycle 90-180 s, and offer Webster auto-timing using Indo-HCM saturation flow per metre so lane-free approaches are timed by width, not lane count. 5) Calibrate the signal discharge so a saturated approach of width w yields roughly the Indo-HCM PCU/h/m value; this is the single best sanity check for the strip/seepage model at junctions. 6) Present any adaptive mode as 'CoSiCoSt-like approximation', because the real algorithm is unpublished
